items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The rise in the cost of producing each additional unit of output in the short run, which explains the upward slope of the supply curve"?
items.answer: increasing marginal cost
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of increasing marginal cost.

items.stem: Distinguish between a movement along the supply curve and a shift of the supply curve.
items.answer: A movement along the curve is caused only by a change in the good's own price; a shift is caused by a non-price determinant such as costs or technology.
items.markingKey: A movement along the curve is caused only by a change in the good's own price; a shift is caused by a non-price determinant such as costs or technology. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between quantity supplied and supply.
items.answer: Supply is the whole relationship between price and quantity supplied (the curve); quantity supplied is the amount offered at one particular price.
items.markingKey: Supply is the whole relationship between price and quantity supplied (the curve); quantity supplied is the amount offered at one particular price. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Outline one way in which US shale oil producers' response to high oil prices from 2010 to 2014 shows the law of supply.
items.answer: With oil prices around $100 a barrel, US shale firms rapidly drilled new wells and US output almost doubled. Higher prices made more costly extraction profitable, so quantity supplied increased.
items.markingKey: Context (With oil prices around $100 a barrel, US shale firms rapidly drilled new wells and US output almost doubled.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Higher prices made more costly extraction profitable, so quantity supplied increased. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the law of supply.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

When the price of avocados in Mexico doubled between 2015 and 2019 because of strong export demand, farmers in Michoacán planted large new orchards, in some cases clearing forests.
— Extract based on news reporting of the avocado boom

Using the extract, explain how the law of supply is illustrated.
items.answer: The higher price made avocado production more profitable, so farmers increased quantity supplied by planting more trees: a positive price-quantity supplied relationship; the forest clearance shows resources moving into the more profitable use.
items.markingKey: The higher price made avocado production more profitable, so farmers increased quantity supplied by planting more trees: a positive price-quantity supplied relationship; the forest clearance shows resources moving into the more profitable use. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: The supply schedules of three producers of mobile phone cases are – Firm B: $2 → 8, $4 → 20, $6 → 26, $8 → 36; Firm D: $2 → 2, $4 → 6, $6 → 8, $8 → 12; Firm A: $2 → 4, $4 → 12, $6 → 15, $8 → 19. Calculate the market quantity supplied at $6 and $8, and explain how the result illustrates the law of supply.
items.markingKey: Horizontal summation gives 49 and 67 [2]; quantity supplied rises with price, a positive relationship ceteris paribus [2].

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of the view that Firms always increase output when the price of their product rises.
items.answer: The law of supply describes a general tendency; the size and speed of response depend on time, capacity and expectations.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: law of supply: higher price raises profit on extra units; new firms are attracted. Arguments against: capacity constraints and time lags (PES low in the short run); firms may expect the price rise to be temporary; regulation, quotas or contracts may prevent expansion. Supported judgement: The law of supply describes a general tendency; the size and speed of response depend on time, capacity and expectations.

items.stem: Explain how a market supply curve is derived from the supply curves of individual firms, and why it shifts when firms leave the industry.
items.answer: Market supply is the horizontal sum of individual firms' quantities supplied at each price; if firms exit, fewer units are supplied at every price, so the market curve shifts left.
items.markingKey: Market supply is the horizontal sum of individual firms' quantities supplied at each price; if firms exit, fewer units are supplied at every price, so the market curve shifts left.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "quantity supplied"?
options: The quantity of a good or service that producers are willing and able to offer for sale at different possible prices in a given time period, ceteris paribus
As more units of a variable factor are added to a fixed factor in the short run, the marginal product of the variable factor eventually falls
A payment by the government to producers per unit of output, which lowers their costs and shifts supply to the right
The amount of a good firms are willing and able to sell at one particular price
items.answer: The amount of a good firms are willing and able to sell at one particular price
items.markingKey: D. "quantity supplied" is the amount of a good firms are willing and able to sell at one particular price.

items.stem: Which of the following best explains why supply curves slope upwards?
options: Higher prices make production more profitable and cover rising marginal costs
Costs of production fall as output rises
Governments require firms to produce more
Consumers buy more at higher prices
items.answer: Higher prices make production more profitable and cover rising marginal costs
items.markingKey: A. Firms increase output when price rises because extra units become profitable despite higher marginal costs.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a shift of the supply curve and a movement along the supply curve.
items.answer: A movement along the curve is caused only by a change in the good's own price; a shift is caused by a non-price determinant such as costs or technology.
items.markingKey: A movement along the curve is caused only by a change in the good's own price; a shift is caused by a non-price determinant such as costs or technology. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims that Firms supply more at higher prices because consumers want more. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Consumers demand less at higher prices; firms supply more because higher prices make extra output profitable and cover rising marginal costs.
items.markingKey: Consumers demand less at higher prices; firms supply more because higher prices make extra output profitable and cover rising marginal costs. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Draw a diagram to illustrate the law of supply and the difference between a change in quantity supplied and a change in supply, and outline what it shows.
items.answer: Diagram: P vs Q, upward-sloping S1. A rise in price from P1 to P2 causes a movement up along S1 from Q1 to Q2 (increase in quantity supplied). A fall in costs of production shifts the curve right from S1 to S2: an increase in supply – more is supplied at every price.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Diagram: P vs Q, upward-sloping S1. A rise in price from P1 to P2 causes a movement up along S1 from Q1 to Q2 (increase in quantity supplied). A fall in costs of production shifts the curve right from S1 to S2: an increase in supply – more is supplied at every price. Award up to 2 marks for an accurate, fully labelled diagram and up to 4 for the explanation linked to it.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim that Higher prices always lead to higher output in the long run.
items.answer: In most markets higher sustained prices raise long-run output, but physical, legal and expectation constraints can limit the response.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: profits attract new firms and investment; supply becomes more elastic over time. Arguments against: natural limits (land, minerals); regulation or quotas restrict output; if high prices are expected to be temporary firms may not invest. Supported judgement: In most markets higher sustained prices raise long-run output, but physical, legal and expectation constraints can limit the response. items.stem: How does an indirect tax affect the supply curve?
options: It shifts the supply curve upwards (to the left) by the amount of the tax
It shifts the demand curve to the left
It causes a movement along the supply curve
It shifts the supply curve downwards by the amount of the tax
items.answer: It shifts the supply curve upwards (to the left) by the amount of the tax
items.markingKey: A. A tax raises firms' costs per unit.

items.stem: A student claims that a rise in demand for a good shifts its supply curve to the right. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: A rise in demand shifts the demand curve, leading to a higher price and a movement along the supply curve (more quantity supplied); the supply curve itself does not shift.
items.markingKey: A rise in demand shifts the demand curve, leading to a higher price and a movement along the supply curve (more quantity supplied); the supply curve itself does not shift. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between joint supply and competitive supply.
items.answer: In joint supply producing one good automatically produces another (beef and leather); in competitive supply resources can produce one good or another, so producing more of one means less of the other (wheat or maize).
items.markingKey: In joint supply producing one good automatically produces another (beef and leather); in competitive supply resources can produce one good or another, so producing more of one means less of the other (wheat or maize). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Read the source below.

Russia and Ukraine together accounted for about 30% of world wheat exports before 2022. After the invasion, Black Sea ports were blockaded and wheat prices on world markets rose to record highs in March 2022.
— Extract based on reporting of grain markets, 2022

Using a supply and demand diagram and the extract, explain why world wheat prices rose.
items.answer: The blockade reduced the quantity of wheat available to world markets, shifting supply left; at the original price there was excess demand, so the equilibrium price rose and quantity traded fell.
items.markingKey: The blockade reduced the quantity of wheat available to world markets, shifting supply left; at the original price there was excess demand, so the equilibrium price rose and quantity traded fell. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: With the help of a labelled diagram, outline the effect of a supply shock in a primary commodity market such as coffee.
items.answer: Diagram: world coffee market; frost destroys crops, shifting supply left from S1 to S2. Excess demand at P1 pushes price up to P2; quantity falls from Q1 to Q2. With inelastic demand the price rise is large relative to the fall in quantity.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Diagram: world coffee market; frost destroys crops, shifting supply left from S1 to S2. Excess demand at P1 pushes price up to P2; quantity falls from Q1 to Q2. With inelastic demand the price rise is large relative to the fall in quantity. Award up to 2 marks for an accurate, fully labelled diagram and up to 4 for the explanation linked to it.

items.stem: Using diagrams, explain the effect on the market for electric cars of (i) a fall in the cost of batteries and (ii) a new government tax on car production.
items.answer: (i) supply shifts right: lower price, higher quantity; (ii) supply shifts left by the tax per unit: higher price, lower quantity. Each diagram: P/Q axes, original S1 and new S2 with new equilibrium.
items.markingKey: (i) supply shifts right: lower price, higher quantity; (ii) supply shifts left by the tax per unit: higher price, lower quantity. Each diagram: P/Q axes, original S1 and new S2 with new equilibrium.

items.stem: Define the term "joint supply".
items.answer: A situation where producing one good automatically produces another, such as beef and leather
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a situation where producing one good automatically produces another, such as beef and leather. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: In the market for bubble tea, which of the following is the effect when many new firms enter the industry, ceteris paribus?
options: Quantity supplied rises along the curve
items.answer: Supply shifts right
items.markingKey: C. Supply shifts right.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a subsidy and an indirect tax.
items.answer: An indirect tax raises firms' costs and shifts supply left/up; a subsidy lowers costs and shifts supply right/down.
items.markingKey: An indirect tax raises firms' costs and shifts supply left/up; a subsidy lowers costs and shifts supply right/down. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between an indirect tax and a subsidy.
items.answer: An indirect tax raises firms' costs and shifts supply left/up; a subsidy lowers costs and shifts supply right/down.
items.markingKey: An indirect tax raises firms' costs and shifts supply left/up; a subsidy lowers costs and shifts supply right/down. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Avian flu led to the culling of over 40 million egg-laying hens in the US in 2022. Explain the effect on the market for eggs.
items.answer: A negative supply shock: supply shifts left, creating excess demand at the original price, so the equilibrium price rises (US egg prices more than doubled) and quantity falls.
items.markingKey: A negative supply shock: supply shifts left, creating excess demand at the original price, so the equilibrium price rises (US egg prices more than doubled) and quantity falls.

items.stem: "Higher wages for workers increase supply because firms have more motivated staff." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Higher wages raise costs of production, which normally shifts supply to the left, unless productivity rises enough to offset them.
items.markingKey: Higher wages raise costs of production, which normally shifts supply to the left, unless productivity rises enough to offset them. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against the view that Indirect taxes on producers are always passed on in full to consumers.
items.answer: Taxes are usually shared; the more inelastic demand is relative to supply, the more is passed to consumers.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: firms raise prices to cover higher costs; true when demand is perfectly inelastic. Arguments against: the incidence depends on PED and PES; with elastic demand producers absorb most of the tax; competition limits price rises. Supported judgement: Taxes are usually shared; the more inelastic demand is relative to supply, the more is passed to consumers.

items.stem: "Technological change is the most important determinant of supply in the long run." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: In the long run technology is usually the dominant force, but in the short run costs, shocks and policy often matter more.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: technology lowers costs and shifts supply right permanently (solar panels, semiconductors); it explains falling real prices of manufactured goods. Arguments against: input costs (energy, wages) drive many supply changes; supply shocks (weather, war) dominate in agriculture; government taxes, subsidies and regulation matter. Supported judgement: In the long run technology is usually the dominant force, but in the short run costs, shocks and policy often matter more. items.stem: In Qs = c + dP, which change represents an increase in supply?
items.answer: An increase in c
items.markingKey: C. A higher c means more is supplied at every price: the curve shifts right.

items.stem: Explain the link between diminishing marginal returns and the upward slope of the supply curve.
items.answer: In the short run, adding workers to fixed capital eventually reduces marginal product, so the cost of each extra unit (marginal cost) rises; firms therefore need a higher price to supply more.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: In the short run, adding workers to fixed capital eventually reduces marginal product, so the cost of each extra unit (marginal cost) rises; firms therefore need a higher price to supply more. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A supply function is Qs = −30 + 6P. Calculate quantity supplied at a price of $15 and the minimum price at which firms will supply.
items.answer: Qs = −30 + 90 = 60; minimum price where Qs = 0: P = $5.
items.markingKey: Qs = −30 + 90 = 60; minimum price where Qs = 0: P = $5.

items.stem: The supply function for streaming subscriptions in Geneva is Qs = −12 + 4P. (a) State the minimum price at which firms supply. (b) A specific tax of $3 per unit is imposed on producers. Write the new supply function and calculate quantity supplied at a market price of $14.
Give one argument for and one argument against the view that Linear supply functions are a reliable way for governments to predict the effects of a tax.
items.answer: Linear functions give useful approximations, especially for small changes, but predictions should be checked against evidence.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: give clear numerical estimates of price and quantity changes; show how incidence depends on the slopes. Arguments against: real supply curves are not linear; firms' costs and technology change; estimates are uncertain. Supported judgement: Linear functions give useful approximations, especially for small changes, but predictions should be checked against evidence.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "linear supply function"?
options: The rise in the cost of producing each additional unit of output in the short run, which explains the upward slope of the supply curve
An equation of the form Qs = c + dP showing quantity supplied as a function of price; d is the change in Qs for each $1 change in price
The extra output produced by employing one more unit of a variable factor such as labour
The sum of the quantities supplied by all firms in a market at each price
items.answer: An equation of the form Qs = c + dP showing quantity supplied as a function of price; d is the change in Qs for each $1 change in price
items.markingKey: B. "linear supply function" is an equation of the form Qs = c + dP showing quantity supplied as a function of price; d is the change in Qs for each $1 change in price.

items.stem: Distinguish between marginal product and average product.
items.answer: Marginal product is the extra output from one more worker; average product is total output divided by the number of workers.
items.markingKey: Marginal product is the extra output from one more worker; average product is total output divided by the number of workers. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims that in Qs = c + dP, a larger d shifts the supply curve to the right. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: d affects the slope (responsiveness of quantity supplied to price); a change in c shifts the curve.
items.markingKey: d affects the slope (responsiveness of quantity supplied to price); a change in c shifts the curve. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: The table shows total output per day for a tailoring workshop with three sewing machines: 1 worker: 12, 2 workers: 31, 3 workers: 51, 4 workers: 69, 5 workers: 81, 6 workers: 88. Calculate the marginal product of each worker and identify the worker after which diminishing marginal returns set in.
items.answer: MP: 12, 19, 20, 18, 12, 7; diminishing returns set in after worker 3
items.markingKey: MP = change in total product: 12, 19, 20, 18, 12, 7 [2]; MP is highest for worker 3 and falls thereafter, so diminishing marginal returns begin after worker 3 [1]; caused by the fixed factor [1].

items.stem: Using a family farm in Kenya adding workers to a fixed plot of land as an example, explain the law of diminishing marginal returns.
items.answer: With a fixed area of land, the first few extra workers greatly increase the tea harvest, but later workers add less because the land becomes crowded. Each extra worker has less land to work with, so marginal product falls even though total output rises.
items.markingKey: Context (With a fixed area of land, the first few extra workers greatly increase the tea harvest, but later workers add less because the land becomes crowded.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Each extra worker has less land to work with, so marginal product falls even though total output rises. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the law of diminishing marginal returns.

items.stem: Draw a diagram to illustrate how the law of diminishing marginal returns leads to an upward-sloping short-run supply curve, and outline what it shows.
items.answer: Diagram 1: output (vertical) against number of workers (horizontal), total product rising at a decreasing rate after a point; marginal product rising then falling. Diagram 2: upward-sloping supply/marginal cost curve: as marginal product falls, marginal cost rises, so higher prices are needed for firms to supply more.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Diagram 1: output (vertical) against number of workers (horizontal), total product rising at a decreasing rate after a point; marginal product rising then falling. Diagram 2: upward-sloping supply/marginal cost curve: as marginal product falls, marginal cost rises, so higher prices are needed for firms to supply more. Award up to 2 marks for an accurate, fully labelled diagram and up to 4 for the explanation linked to it.

items.stem: A supply function changes from Qs = −40 + 5P to Qs = −10 + 5P. Explain what might have caused this, calculate the change in quantity supplied at a price of $12 and describe the change on a diagram.
items.answer: c rose from −40 to −10: e.g. lower input costs or better technology; at P = 12, Qs rises from 20 to 50 (+30); parallel shift of the supply curve to the right; price intercept falls from $8 to $2.
items.markingKey: c rose from −40 to −10: e.g. lower input costs or better technology; at P = 12, Qs rises from 20 to 50 (+30); parallel shift of the supply curve to the right; price intercept falls from $8 to $2.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "law of supply"?
options: The positive relationship between the price of a good and the quantity supplied, ceteris paribus
An unexpected event, such as a natural disaster, war or disease, that suddenly changes the supply of a good
The extra output produced by employing one more unit of a variable factor such as labour
The period in which at least one factor of production is fixed
items.answer: The positive relationship between the price of a good and the quantity supplied, ceteris paribus
items.markingKey: A. "law of supply" is the positive relationship between the price of a good and the quantity supplied, ceteris paribus.

The sum of the quantities supplied by all firms in a market at each price
The period in which at least one factor of production is fixed
items.answer: Factors other than the good's own price that shift the supply curve: costs of factors of production, technology, prices of related goods, expectations, indirect taxes and subsidies, the number of firms and supply shocks
items.markingKey: B. "non-price determinants of supply" is factors other than the good's own price that shift the supply curve: costs of factors of production, technology, prices of related goods, expectations, indirect taxes and subsidies, the number of firms and supply shocks.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The period in which at least one factor of production is fixed"?
items.answer: short run
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of short run.

items.stem: Explain why a higher price gives firms an incentive to increase quantity supplied.
items.answer: At a higher price each unit earns more revenue; output that was previously unprofitable now covers its (rising) marginal cost, so profit-maximising firms expand production and new resources are attracted into the industry.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: At a higher price each unit earns more revenue; output that was previously unprofitable now covers its (rising) marginal cost, so profit-maximising firms expand production and new resources are attracted into the industry. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why an improvement in technology shifts the supply curve to the right.
items.answer: New technology raises productivity and lowers the cost per unit, so firms can profitably supply more at every price.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: New technology raises productivity and lowers the cost per unit, so firms can profitably supply more at every price. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly explain why diminishing returns only occur in the short run.
items.answer: They arise because at least one factor is fixed; in the long run all factors can be varied, so the firm can expand capital along with labour.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They arise because at least one factor is fixed; in the long run all factors can be varied, so the firm can expand capital along with labour. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.answer: Supply is the whole relationship between price and quantity supplied (the curve); quantity supplied is the amount offered at one particular price.

items.stem: Explain why an expected rise in the future price of a good may reduce its supply today.
items.answer: If producers expect higher prices later (e.g. oil or grain), they may hold back stocks to sell later, reducing current supply at every price.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: If producers expect higher prices later (e.g. oil or grain), they may hold back stocks to sell later, reducing current supply at every price. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between diminishing marginal returns and diseconomies of scale.
items.answer: Diminishing returns is a short-run concept: adding a variable factor to a fixed factor reduces marginal product. Diseconomies of scale are a long-run concept: average costs rise as the scale of all inputs increases.
items.markingKey: Diminishing returns is a short-run concept: adding a variable factor to a fixed factor reduces marginal product. Diseconomies of scale are a long-run concept: average costs rise as the scale of all inputs increases. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: The world price of cocoa rose sharply in 2024. Explain the likely response of cocoa farmers in Côte d'Ivoire in the short run and in the long run.
items.answer: Short run: limited increase in quantity supplied (better harvesting, using stocks) – a movement along a steep supply curve; long run: farmers plant more trees and new land is brought into cocoa, so quantity supplied rises more as supply becomes more elastic.
items.markingKey: Short run: limited increase in quantity supplied (better harvesting, using stocks) – a movement along a steep supply curve; long run: farmers plant more trees and new land is brought into cocoa, so quantity supplied rises more as supply becomes more elastic.

items.stem: With the help of a labelled diagram, outline the law of supply and the difference between a change in quantity supplied and a change in supply.
items.answer: Diagram: P vs Q, upward-sloping S1. A rise in price from P1 to P2 causes a movement up along S1 from Q1 to Q2 (increase in quantity supplied). A fall in costs of production shifts the curve right from S1 to S2: an increase in supply – more is supplied at every price.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Diagram: P vs Q, upward-sloping S1. A rise in price from P1 to P2 causes a movement up along S1 from Q1 to Q2 (increase in quantity supplied). A fall in costs of production shifts the curve right from S1 to S2: an increase in supply – more is supplied at every price. Award up to 2 marks for an accurate, fully labelled diagram and up to 4 for the explanation linked to it.

items.stem: "A rise in demand for a good shifts its supply curve to the right." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: A rise in demand shifts the demand curve, leading to a higher price and a movement along the supply curve (more quantity supplied); the supply curve itself does not shift.
items.markingKey: A rise in demand shifts the demand curve, leading to a higher price and a movement along the supply curve (more quantity supplied); the supply curve itself does not shift. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With reference to a family farm in Kenya adding workers to a fixed plot of land, explain how it illustrates the law of diminishing marginal returns.
items.answer: With a fixed area of land, the first few extra workers greatly increase the tea harvest, but later workers add less because the land becomes crowded. Each extra worker has less land to work with, so marginal product falls even though total output rises.
items.markingKey: Context (With a fixed area of land, the first few extra workers greatly increase the tea harvest, but later workers add less because the land becomes crowded.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Each extra worker has less land to work with, so marginal product falls even though total output rises. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the law of diminishing marginal returns.

items.stem: Using US shale oil producers' response to high oil prices from 2010 to 2014 as an example, explain the law of supply.
items.answer: With oil prices around $100 a barrel, US shale firms rapidly drilled new wells and US output almost doubled. Higher prices made more costly extraction profitable, so quantity supplied increased.
items.markingKey: Context (With oil prices around $100 a barrel, US shale firms rapidly drilled new wells and US output almost doubled.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Higher prices made more costly extraction profitable, so quantity supplied increased. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the law of supply.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of the view that Indirect taxes on producers are always passed on in full to consumers.
items.answer: Taxes are usually shared; the more inelastic demand is relative to supply, the more is passed to consumers.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: firms raise prices to cover higher costs; true when demand is perfectly inelastic. Arguments against: the incidence depends on PED and PES; with elastic demand producers absorb most of the tax; competition limits price rises. Supported judgement: Taxes are usually shared; the more inelastic demand is relative to supply, the more is passed to consumers.

items.stem: To what extent is it true that Linear supply functions are a reliable way for governments to predict the effects of a tax?
items.answer: Linear functions give useful approximations, especially for small changes, but predictions should be checked against evidence.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: give clear numerical estimates of price and quantity changes; show how incidence depends on the slopes. Arguments against: real supply curves are not linear; firms' costs and technology change; estimates are uncertain. Supported judgement: Linear functions give useful approximations, especially for small changes, but predictions should be checked against evidence. items.stem: To what extent is it true that Higher prices always lead to higher output in the long run?
items.answer: In most markets higher sustained prices raise long-run output, but physical, legal and expectation constraints can limit the response.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: profits attract new firms and investment; supply becomes more elastic over time. Arguments against: natural limits (land, minerals); regulation or quotas restrict output; if high prices are expected to be temporary firms may not invest. Supported judgement: In most markets higher sustained prices raise long-run output, but physical, legal and expectation constraints can limit the response. items.stem: Using real-world examples, discuss the claim that technological change is the most important determinant of supply in the long run.
items.answer: In the long run technology is usually the dominant force, but in the short run costs, shocks and policy often matter more.

items.stem: Lars writes: "When the price of a good rises, supply increases." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: A rise in the good's own price increases the quantity supplied – a movement up along the supply curve; supply (the curve) shifts only if a non-price determinant changes.
items.markingKey: A rise in the good's own price increases the quantity supplied – a movement up along the supply curve; supply (the curve) shifts only if a non-price determinant changes. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between an indirect tax and a subsidy.
items.answer: An indirect tax raises firms' costs and shifts supply left/up; a subsidy lowers costs and shifts supply right/down.
items.markingKey: An indirect tax raises firms' costs and shifts supply left/up; a subsidy lowers costs and shifts supply right/down. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between diseconomies of scale and diminishing marginal returns.
items.answer: Diminishing returns is a short-run concept: adding a variable factor to a fixed factor reduces marginal product. Diseconomies of scale are a long-run concept: average costs rise as the scale of all inputs increases.
items.markingKey: Diminishing returns is a short-run concept: adding a variable factor to a fixed factor reduces marginal product. Diseconomies of scale are a long-run concept: average costs rise as the scale of all inputs increases. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why market supply increases when new firms enter an industry.
items.answer: Market supply is the sum of all firms' quantities; more firms means more is supplied at each price, so the curve shifts right.
